blocks.recap_md: A procedure definition like `(define (square x) (* x x))` creates a compound procedure named `square`, where `x` is a formal parameter standing for whatever argument it's applied to.
The general form is `(define (⟨name⟩ ⟨formal parameters⟩) ⟨body⟩)`; the body yields the procedure's value once the formal parameters are replaced by actual arguments.
`square` is used to build `sum-of-squares` (x^2 + y^2), showing how a compound procedure becomes a building block for another.
`sum-of-squares` in turn becomes a building block for `f`; compound procedures are used exactly like primitive ones, indistinguishably.

knowledge_items.statement: A procedure definition like `(define (square x) (* x x))` creates a compound procedure named `square`, where `x` is a formal parameter: a local name for whatever argument the procedure is applied to.

The general form of a procedure definition is `(define (⟨name⟩ ⟨formal parameters⟩) ⟨body⟩)`: the body is an expression that yields the procedure's value once the formal parameters are replaced by the actual arguments.

Compound procedures can be used as building blocks for defining further compound procedures (e.g. `sum-of-squares` built from `square`, then `f` built from `sum-of-squares`), and are used exactly the same way as primitive procedures - there's no way to tell from how a procedure is used whether it's built in or user-defined.

questions.prompt: In `(define (square x) (* x x))`, what role does `x` play?
options: It's a formal parameter: a local name standing for whatever argument `square` is applied to, similar to how a pronoun stands in for a noun
It's a global variable that must already have a numeric value before this definition is evaluated
It's the name of the procedure itself; `square` is just a comment
It's a fixed constant equal to 1, used as a placeholder
questions.explanation: The text compares the formal parameter to a pronoun in natural language: `x` names 'the thing to be multiplied' generically, and gets replaced by the actual argument each time `square` is applied - it isn't a global variable or a constant.

questions.prompt: In the general form `(define (⟨name⟩ ⟨formal parameters⟩) ⟨body⟩)`, when does the body's expression actually get evaluated to produce a value?
options: When the procedure is applied, with the formal parameters replaced by the actual arguments of that application
Immediately, at the moment the `define` itself is evaluated, using whatever values the formal parameters currently hold
Only the first time the procedure is ever called; later calls reuse that first cached result
Never automatically - the body must be evaluated manually afterward with a separate command
questions.explanation: Defining a procedure just creates and names it; the body is an expression that yields the procedure application's value once the formal parameters are replaced by the actual arguments of a specific call - evaluating `define` itself doesn't run the body.

questions.prompt: Looking only at the definition of `sum-of-squares`, which calls `square`, can you tell whether `square` is a primitive built into the interpreter or a compound procedure the user defined?
options: No - compound procedures are used exactly the same way as primitive procedures, so the definition alone doesn't reveal which `square` is
Yes - compound procedures always require an extra keyword like `compound` before their name
Yes - only primitive procedures can appear inside another procedure's body
Yes - primitive procedures never take exactly one argument the way `square` does
questions.explanation: The text says exactly this: one could not tell by looking at the definition of sum-of-squares whether square was built into the interpreter or defined as a compound procedure - compound and primitive procedures are indistinguishable in use.
